newsitem.title: UK: British leader wanted Uganda's Amin killed - paper.
newsitem.headline: British leader wanted Uganda's Amin killed - paper.

text.p: Former British Prime Minister Harold Wilson was so worried by mass killings in Uganda during Idi Amin's rule that he asked the Foreign Office whether it could arrange the dictator's assassination, a newspaper said on Wednesday.
The Independent quoted the late leader's former press secretary Joe Haines as saying Wilson abandoned the idea in the face of strong resistance from the Foreign Office.

The daily said Haines had told the makers of a BBC documentary that Wilson came up with the idea of killing Amin in the mid 1970s when the dictator's forces were said to be massacring 7,000 people a week.
An estimated 500,000 people were slaughtered during Amin's rule from 1971 to 1979, many by state security agencies.

"Harold called me up to his study and said that he was very concerned about this. He asked me on my view about killing Idi Amin, as he thought that was the only way of stopping the slaiughter," the newspaper quoted Haines as saying.

"I was against capital punishment, but I said that in this case we should make an exception. He was very concerned...and he told me he was going to take the idea up with the Foreign Office," said Haines, who described Amin as a madman.
"I don't know who (Wilson talked to), but he told me later that the Foreign Office was scared out of its life."
Wilson, who served as prime minister four times, died in 1985.
Haines said the Foreign Office strongly opposed the idea for fear the Ugandans might retaliate by launching an assassination attempt of their own in Britain.
In 1977 the International Commission of Jurists said Amin had violated every fundamental human right during his "reign of terror". Amin now lives in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.
